passage: The rain had trapped everyone under the bus shelter, and the bus was late. Hansa, five, had discovered the concrete step at the edge. She stood on it, bent her knees, and jumped down with both feet. Splash! "I did it! Rukmini Masi, look!" She climbed back up. Jump. "Again!" Up. Jump. "Again!" Her frock was soaked at the hem. Masi held the umbrella over the step and counted each jump out loud. By the time the bus came, Hansa had jumped nineteen times, and she climbed on grinning, still bending her knees.

qa.q: How many times had Hansa jumped by the time the bus came?
qa.a: Hansa had jumped nineteen times.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep shouting 'Again!'?
qa.a: Each jump made her feel able and proud, and that good feeling made her want to do it over and over 😊.

qa.q: What did Rukmini Masi choose to do in the rain, and why did it help?
qa.a: She held the umbrella over the step and counted each jump, making Hansa's new skill feel seen and safe to practise.

qa.q: What might the other people at the shelter think, watching Hansa?
qa.a: They might smile at the small girl's delight, which makes the late bus and the rain a little easier to bear.

grounding: A five-year-old proudly jumps off a step in the rain and asks to do it again and again.

passage: In their Kochi apartment building, Elizabeth aunty from the flat next door was blowing up balloons for her son's birthday. Salma sat beside her on the stairs, watching. "Can I tie one?" Elizabeth aunty showed her: wrap, tuck, pull. The first balloon whooshed out of Salma's fingers and flew down the stairs. The second one too. On the third try, the knot held. Salma held it up with both hands, eyes huge. "I tied it! Me!" She grabbed another balloon. "Blow this one! I'll tie!" She tied eleven balloons that afternoon, each a bit lopsided, and after every single knot she said, "Look, aunty. Look."

qa.q: How many balloons did Salma tie that afternoon?
qa.a: She tied eleven balloons, each a bit lopsided.

qa.q: What does 'I tied it! Me!' with huge eyes tell us about how Salma felt?
qa.a: She felt amazed and proud of her new skill, and that pride made her want to tie every balloon.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth aunty make after the first two balloons flew away?
qa.a: She let Salma keep trying instead of taking over, so Salma could feel the knot finally hold on her own.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth aunty feel hearing 'Look, aunty. Look.' after every knot?
qa.a: She may feel warm and a little amused, sharing a child's pride in something grown-ups do without thinking 😊.

grounding: A small girl learns to tie a balloon knot and proudly repeats it again and again.

passage:
'Mummy! Mummy! Watch!' Deepak stood on the second stair, knees bent.
'I'm watching,' said Mahima, drying her hands on a towel.
He jumped. Thump! Both feet on the floor. He wobbled, but didn't fall.
'I did it! From the SECOND one!'
'You did! Wah!'
'Again!' He climbed back up. 'Watch again!'
Thump!
Papa came out of the bathroom. 'What's all the noise?'
'Papa, I can jump from the second stair! Watch me!'
'Hmm, show me.'
Thump! Deepak threw his arms up. 'Now the third one?'
Mahima laughed. 'Tomorrow, the third one. Today you've done the second twenty times.'

qa.q: Which stair did Deepak jump from?
qa.a: From the second stair, landing with both feet on the floor.

qa.q: Why did Deepak want Papa to watch too?
qa.a: He was so proud of his new jump that he wanted everyone to see it and share how able he felt.

qa.q: What did Mahima decide about the third stair, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: She said 'Tomorrow, the third one', keeping his excitement alive while letting him enjoy mastering the second step first.

qa.q: What is it like for Mahima to hear 'Again!' so many times?
qa.a: Mahima may feel a bit tired of watching but also delighted, seeing how proud her son is of his new jump.

grounding: A little boy proudly jumps from the second stair and asks his parents to watch again and again.

passage:
Preschool note, Friday. Neelam.
Today Gargi (5) tied her first proper knot on the lacing card, a real double knot. She held it up to me with both hands. 'Look! Look! I did it!'
Then she pulled it loose and did it again. And again. Seven times, counting out loud. Each time she checked my face.
She asked to take a shoelace home 'to practise on Papa's shoes'. I gave her one.
Plan for next week: bows. She's ready, and she wants it.

qa.q: How many times did Gargi tie the knot?
qa.a: Seven times, counting out loud.

qa.q: Why did Gargi keep untying and retying the knot?
qa.a: She felt proud of being able to do it and wanted that feeling again and again; each success made her want to try more.

qa.q: What choice did Neelam make that fed Gargi's eagerness?
qa.a: Neelam gave her a shoelace to take home and planned bows for next week, building on her pride with the next small challenge.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Gargi practises knots on his shoes?
qa.a: Papa may be amused and proud, perhaps finding his shoes knotted, but seeing how excited Gargi is to show a new skill.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child who proudly ties her first knot and wants to do it again and again.

passage:
At the ghat steps near the temple in their small town, Kamal stood on the second step, knees bent, fists tight. The step below looked very far away.
'Jump, Kamal!' called his didi, Sukanya, holding the flower basket.
He jumped. He landed on both feet, wobbled, and didn't fall. His mouth fell open. 'Didi! I jumped the big one!'
Before she could answer, he climbed back up. Jump. Again. Again. Each time he shouted, 'Did you see?'
Sukanya put the basket down and counted for him. By eleven, the old priest sweeping the steps was counting too.

qa.q: Who was sweeping the steps?
qa.a: The old priest.

qa.q: How can you tell Kamal felt proud after the first jump?
qa.a: His mouth fell open, he shouted 'I jumped the big one!' and climbed straight back up to do it again.

qa.q: What choice of Sukanya's helped Kamal keep practising?
qa.a: She put the basket down and counted his jumps, noticing each one, which fed his pride and his effort.

qa.q: What might the old priest have enjoyed in joining the counting?
qa.a: The priest probably enjoyed Kamal's delight and wanted to share in it, adding another pair of eyes to his proud jumps. 🙂

grounding: A young child proudly jumps a big step and wants to do it again and again, the feeling of being able driving him on.

passage: In the small kitchen in Prague, Jana sat on the floor with her sneaker in her lap. Loop, wrap, pull. The lace slipped. Loop, wrap, pull. And then, suddenly, a real bow. She gasped. 'Tati! Look!' Her father, Mateo, looked. 'You tied it!' Jana pulled the bow undone. 'Again. Watch again.' She tied it, slower this time, tongue out. 'Again!' By dinner she had tied and untied that shoe eleven times, and made her father count every one.

qa.q: How many times did Jana tie and untie the shoe by dinner?
qa.a: She tied and untied it eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Jana keep untying the bow to do it again?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited about her new skill, and doing it again let her feel that pride each time.

qa.q: What could Mateo do to support Jana's new skill?
qa.a: Watch and count with her, and later offer the other shoe or a new knot, so the feeling of being able keeps growing.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mateo to count eleven times?
qa.a: Mateo might feel amused and a little tired, but also proud to see her so delighted.

grounding: A young child ties her first bow and proudly asks to do it again and again, her new ability fuelling more effort.

passage: At the preschool, the new step-block had two stairs, and for a week Sabina had only climbed down holding the rail. This morning she stood on the top step, bent her knees, and jumped. She landed with both feet flat on the mat. Her eyes went big. 'Dolma Ma'am! I jumped!' 'You did,' said Dolma Ma'am, smiling. Sabina climbed straight back up. 'Watch! Watch!' She jumped again. And again. Each time she landed she shouted 'I did it!' as though it were the very first time. She jumped fourteen times before snack.

qa.q: How many times did Sabina jump before snack?
qa.a: She jumped fourteen times before snack.

qa.q: Why did Sabina shout 'I did it!' every time?
qa.a: She felt proud and thrilled with her new skill, and each jump brought back the joy of being able to do it.

qa.q: How can a teacher build on this pride?
qa.a: By watching and naming what she did, and later offering a slightly harder challenge, so her sense of being able keeps growing.

qa.q: How might Dolma Ma'am feel watching the fourteen jumps?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy and amused, seeing Sabina's confidence grow.

grounding: A young child jumps off a step for the first time and proudly repeats it again and again.

passage:
Monday. Manjula tried to button her school shirt and cried when the buttons wouldn't go in. Her sister Jasleen did them for her.
Wednesday. Manjula practised on Jasleen's old cardigan, one big button at a time, while Jasleen did her homework. She got two in and shouted, 'Two!'
Friday. Manjula buttoned her whole school shirt by herself, top to bottom. She stood very tall. Then she unbuttoned it. 'Watch me do it again!' She did it three times before breakfast, was nearly late, and didn't mind at all.

qa.q: What did Manjula practise on?
qa.a: She practised on Jasleen's old cardigan.

qa.q: Why did Manjula unbutton the shirt to do it again?
qa.a: She felt proud and excited about her new skill, so doing it again let her enjoy feeling able.

qa.q: What helped Manjula learn buttoning?
qa.a: Practising on a cardigan with big buttons, one at a time, gave her small wins before the harder school shirt.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel on Friday?
qa.a: Jasleen would likely feel proud of her sister, and maybe relieved not to be doing the buttons anymore.

grounding: Over a week, a young child learns to button her shirt and proudly repeats it, her new ability fuelling more effort.

passage:
It was Holi morning. The courtyard was wet and slippery with coloured water, and cousin Jagdish was shouting, “Careful, Simran!”
Simran, five, stood at the top of the three stone steps. For weeks she had jumped only from the lowest one.
She bent her knees. Jumped. Landed on both feet, splashing pink water everywhere.
She gasped. Then she laughed out loud.
“Again!” She ran back up. Jumped. Again. Again.
Jagdish gave up and just held out his hand at the bottom each time.
By the tenth jump, Simran was pink to the knees and grinning so hard her cheeks hurt.

qa.q: How many stone steps did Simran jump from?
qa.a: She jumped from the top of three stone steps.

qa.q: How did Simran feel after the first jump from the top?
qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, laughing out loud because she could do something new.

qa.q: How did Jagdish keep her safe while letting her practise?
qa.a: He held out his hand at the bottom each time instead of stopping her.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel watching her jump again and again?
qa.a: Jagdish probably felt worried about the slippery courtyard at first, then amused and happy for her.

grounding: The passage shows a young child proudly jumping a new step on a slippery Holi morning and asking to do it again and again.

passage:
It was Diwali cleaning week, and the flat smelled of dust and polish. Vaibhav, five, sat in the corridor with his school shoes.
His big sister Kashish showed him once more. “Loop, round, pull through.”
Vaibhav's tongue stuck out. Loop. Round. Pull through.
A knot. A real knot.
“Didi! Look!”
Kashish looked. “Wow!”
He pulled it undone and tied it again. And again. Then he tied Kashish's sneaker. Then Papa's shoe.
Mumma called for help with the diyas, but Vaibhav shouted, “One more!” He tied his shoe six more times before he came.

qa.q: How many more times did Vaibhav tie his shoe before he came?
qa.a: He tied his shoe six more times.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he tied his first real knot?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud, calling out to Didi to look.

qa.q: How could the family keep his effort going?
qa.a: They could let him help tie everyone's shoes, giving him chances to use his new skill.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel seeing him tie again and again?
qa.a: Kashish probably feels happy and proud that her teaching worked.

grounding: The passage shows a young child proudly tying his first knot during festival cleaning and wanting to repeat it again and again.

passage:
“Maria Aunty, can I tie the ribbon?” It was Christmas Eve, and Aunty's flat was full of gifts and paper.
“Try, Parveen. Make two bunny ears.”
“Bunny ears… cross… through…” A pause. “Aunty! It's a bow!”
“It is! A perfect bow.”
“Can I do another one?”
“Of course.”
“And another?”
“There are twelve gifts, sweetheart.”
“I'll do all twelve!”
Twelve bows later, some lopsided, Parveen held up the last one. “I can do bows now. Forever.”
“Forever,” Maria Aunty agreed, smiling.

qa.q: How many gifts were there to tie ribbons on?
qa.a: There were twelve gifts.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when the first bow worked?
qa.a: She felt excited and proud, shouting “Aunty! It's a bow!” and asking to do more.

qa.q: What did Maria Aunty do that encouraged Parveen?
qa.a: She gave a simple tip, praised the first bow and let Parveen try all twelve, even the lopsided ones.

qa.q: How might Maria Aunty feel hearing “I can do bows now. Forever”?
qa.a: She probably feels warm and amused, glad to see Parveen so proud.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young child proudly tying her first ribbon bows at Christmas and asking to do it again and again.

passage:
Preschool note, winter term, by Eshaan
Today Samir tied a knot in his scarf for the first time. He'd been trying all week. When it held, he gasped and held it up. "Look! Look!" Then he untied it and tied it again. And again. Seven times. Each time he looked at me and grinned. At going-home time he showed his mother. "I can do knots!"
What I did next: I gave him a piece of rope to practise knots at the play corner tomorrow. 🙂

qa.a: Seven times.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when the knot held?
qa.a: Samir felt proud and excited, gasping and holding it up to show.

qa.q: Why was giving Samir a piece of rope a good idea?
qa.a: It lets him keep practising a skill he feels proud of, which keeps his effort going.

qa.q: How might Samir's mother have felt when he said "I can do knots!"?
qa.a: She was probably happy and proud to see her son so excited.

grounding: A preschool note shows a small boy proudly tying his first knot and asking to do it again and again.

passage: After the monsoon rain, a big puddle lay in front of the village house. Kiran stood at the edge. Arnab Dadu watched from the veranda. Kiran bent her knees, swung her arms, and jumped. She landed on the other side, only one foot wet. "Dadu! I jumped it!" She ran back round and jumped again. And again. Each time she shouted, "Watch, Dadu!" Her frock got muddy. Dadu laughed. "Again?" "Again!" On the tenth jump, she landed with both feet dry. She stood very still, then threw her arms up. "I'm the best jumper!"

qa.q: Who watched Kiran from the veranda?
qa.a: Arnab Dadu watched from the veranda.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after each jump?
qa.a: Kiran felt proud and joyful, shouting to Dadu and wanting to do it again.

qa.q: Why is Dadu's watching and laughing helpful?
qa.a: It lets Kiran enjoy her new skill without pressure, which keeps her keen to keep trying.

qa.q: How might Dadu feel watching Kiran jump ten times?
qa.a: Dadu seemed amused and happy, enjoying her pride and energy.

grounding: After monsoon rain a small girl proudly jumps a puddle and asks to do it again and again, feeling able.

passage: On Christmas Eve in Madrid, Sofia, four, stood on the bottom step of the stairs to the neighbour's door. Her mother Vera held out a hand. Sofia shook her head. "No hand!" She jumped down with both feet together. She wobbled, but stayed up. Her mouth fell open. "Mamá! I jumped!" She climbed back up and jumped again. Then again. Then from the second step. Vera held her breath, then smiled. "Again, Mamá, watch!" By the time the neighbours opened the door, Sofia had jumped fifteen times and her cheeks were pink with pride.

qa.q: How many times had Sofia jumped by the time the neighbours opened the door?
qa.a: Sofia had jumped fifteen times.

qa.q: How did Sofia feel after her first jump?
qa.a: Sofia felt amazed and proud, her mouth falling open as she shouted to Mamá.

qa.q: What did Vera do that helped Sofia's new skill grow?
qa.a: She let Sofia jump without her hand and watched each time, so Sofia could feel able and keep trying.

qa.q: What might Vera have felt when Sofia tried from the second step?
qa.a: Vera felt nervous, holding her breath, then relieved and proud when Sofia landed.

grounding: On Christmas Eve a small girl proudly jumps down a step and asks to do it again and again, feeling able.

He looked up at Gopika Miss, eyes huge. "I jumped! Again!"
